Bitcoin ATM Scam UK: Why a Caller Sending You to One Is a Scam

No genuine bank, HMRC officer, or tech-support agent will direct you to a Bitcoin ATM. Treat that instruction as a scam, whatever the caller says.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-05-05 · Updated 2026-07-10 · 4 min read

Bitcoin ATM scam UKcrypto ATM illegal UKFCA crypto ATMBitcoin ATM fraudis Bitcoin ATM illegal UKcryptocurrency scam UKcrypto fraud UK
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.

What the Bitcoin ATM scam looks like

This scam is a phone call, text, or email — usually claiming to be your bank's fraud team, HMRC, or a tech-support agent — that convinces you your money or device is at risk and the only fix is to withdraw cash and feed it into a Bitcoin ATM.

An example of the style: To secure your account, withdraw £3,000 and deposit it at your nearest Bitcoin machine using this QR code. The machines themselves are physical kiosks that convert cash to cryptocurrency, but the scam is the instruction: no genuine bank, HMRC contact, or legitimate support service will ask you to use one to protect money or fix an account.

Why the FCA treats crypto ATMs as high risk

Any business that runs a cryptoasset ATM in the UK must register with the FCA under the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds Regulations 2017. The FCA has taken enforcement action against unregistered crypto ATMs and has warned consumers not to use illegal machines. Because registration status can change, check the FCA's current register directly if you are ever unsure, but never use any crypto ATM because an unexpected caller, texter, or "support" contact told you to.

Warning signs of the scam

  • An unexpected call, text, or email claims a problem with your bank account, tax affairs, or computer, and creates urgency to act immediately.
  • You're told to withdraw cash and convert it to cryptocurrency at a Bitcoin ATM to "secure", "verify", or "protect" your money.
  • You're given a QR code or wallet address to scan or enter at the machine, described as a "safe", "holding", or "verification" account.
  • You're asked to stay on the phone throughout, or told not to mention the real reason for the payment to anyone, including staff near the machine.
  • The caller can quote your name, and sometimes partial account details, but cannot be verified independently — this proves nothing, since such details are often obtained from data breaches.
  • No genuine bank, HMRC officer, or tech-support agent will ever direct you to a Bitcoin ATM.

How to check a call like this is genuine

Hang up and contact the organisation yourself, using the number on your card, a genuine bill, or their official website — never a number given to you by the caller. Genuine banks, HMRC, and legitimate tech-support services never ask you to withdraw cash and convert it to cryptocurrency at an ATM, under any circumstances; treat that instruction alone as conclusive proof of a scam, regardless of how convincing the caller sounds. Check your real account directly through your bank's app or by logging into it independently, rather than trusting anything the caller tells you about it.

If you're also asked to visit a link, see Is This Website a Scam? A Practical Checklist Before You Buy.

What to do if you've already used one

Stop all contact with the caller immediately — do not send anything further, even if told an extra payment will reverse the transaction. Contact your bank straight away to explain what happened; while cryptocurrency itself typically can't be recovered once sent, your bank can flag your account and watch for further fraud, and the venue or ATM operator may hold camera footage worth preserving. Report the wallet address you sent funds to, along with the phone number and any messages, to Report Fraud — this helps investigators trace and disrupt the network even when your own funds can't be recovered.

How to report a Bitcoin ATM scam in the UK

Report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 if you're in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, with the wallet address, phone number, and machine location. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101. If contact came by email, forward it to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk; by text, forward it free to 7726.

Frequently asked questions

Are Bitcoin ATMs legal in the UK?

Cryptoasset ATM operators must be registered with the FCA under UK money-laundering rules, and the FCA has taken action against unregistered machines. Check the FCA's current register directly if you need to verify a business, but a caller telling you to use a Bitcoin ATM is enough on its own to treat the contact as a scam.

My bank/HMRC/tech support told me to use a Bitcoin ATM to fix a problem — is that genuine?

No. No genuine UK bank, HMRC officer, or legitimate tech-support service will ever ask you to withdraw cash and feed it into a Bitcoin ATM for any reason. This instruction is on its own enough to confirm a scam — hang up and contact the real organisation using a number you find independently.

I've already sent money through a Bitcoin ATM to a scammer — can I get it back?

It's very difficult, since cryptocurrency sent to a scammer's wallet typically can't be reversed. Contact your bank to flag your account, and report the wallet address and phone number to Report Fraud — this won't usually recover your funds but helps investigators build a picture of the network.

How do I report a Bitcoin ATM scam?

Report to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland), including the wallet address and phone number used. Forward a related email to report@phishing.gov.uk or a text to 7726.
